articles.title: When the tap runs dry: Women carry more than water in Kazakhstan
articles.summary: When a woman learns to calculate the value of her time and says, “This is evidence, and they must answer,” a permanent shift takes place for her and the community.
articles.content:
This article was produced by Nazgul Aidabossynova from Kazakhstan through the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In the village of Qyzylsay, southern Kazakhstan, the water disappears every afternoon. This is not a metaphor. By noon, the pipes literally go dry.

Women wake before dawn to fill every container they own. Then they wait for the water to return. And while they wait, they carry buckets to gardens, feed livestock, take children to school, and shoulder an invisible mountain of labor that nobody counts, nobody pays for, and nobody sees. Ten women decided to change that.

The problem nobody counted

Qyzylsay sits in one of the hottest corners of Kazakhstan. Summers here now break records that old-timers say didn’t exist 20 years ago. According to Kazakhstan’s own data, water losses reach 40–60 percent in rural areas. Many rural areas also lack adequate sanitation infrastructure, according to research from The Borgen Project, so even when there is water, it isn’t always safe to drink. For the women of Qyzylsay, this is not a statistic. It is the silence of an empty tap at midday.

In June 2026, UN Women released its landmark report “Progress of the World’s Women 2026: Gender Equality in the Age of Climate Crisis.” It stated plainly what women in Qyzylsay already knew in their bones. You cannot build sustainable agriculture, or any sustainable future, without integrating the “care economy” into climate and agricultural planning.

Rural women bear the heaviest burden of energy shortages, physical labor, and livestock care. The result is that they have almost no time to learn, to earn, or to organize.

Rural women in Kazakhstan work 10 to 15 hours per day, most of it uncounted and unpaid. In Qyzylsay, that labor includes waking at 4 a.m. on irrigation days to stand in a field for five hours watching water flow through irrigation channels. If you miss your turn to water, your garden dies. Five hours, three times a week: Forty to 60 hours a month, trapped in one of the lowest-value tasks imaginable.

A phone that does more than WhatsApp

My name is Nazgul, and from May to June 2026, I led four trainings for women in Qyzylsay under a project called “Digital Voice of Qyzylsay Women.” The premise was simple: Most women in this community already had smartphones. What they lacked was the knowledge that those phones could do more than send messages.



We started with the basics: Reminders for livestock care, farm diaries with photographs, and training on the eGov app, which lets you request official government documents without traveling to the city.

For women who had stood in queues for hours at government offices just to get a birth certificate, this was not a convenience. It was a revelation.



Then we moved to water.

Evidence that cannot be ignored

Training 2 was called “Smart Water: When Your Garden Tells You It’s Thirsty.” We taught participants how to photograph water problems, such as dry canals, broken pipes, and contaminated sources, with automatic timestamps. We called these “Water Problem Cards.” A photo without metadata is an opinion. A photo with GPS coordinates, a date, and a description is evidence.

We talked about Kazakhstan’s water rights in plain language, not legal jargon. Most of the women had never heard that access to clean water is not a favor from the local government, but a legal right.

One of the participants said: “I always thought they ignored us because they could. Now I know they ignore us because we don’t have proof. So now we’ll have proof.”

The number that changed everything

Training 3 hit hardest. We sat together and calculated the true cost of one liter of milk — including the woman’s own time at a minimum wage rate. The room went quiet when participants realized they were subsidizing their buyers. They were running charities, not businesses.



We also calculated what smart irrigation automation could return: 60 hours per month. Sixty hours that could be used for market trips, online courses, rest, or civic participation. At KZT 500 (USD 1.09) per hour, that is KZT 30,000 (USD 65.17) over one growing season — enough to pay back a shared automated pump system.

By Training 4, the conversation had shifted. We were no longer talking about individual phones. We were talking about collective power.

The most important outcome of these four months was not digital literacy. It was trust. The women participants who had worked alongside each other for years decided to form a cooperative.



It has multiple founding purposes: to collectively address the village’s water supply crisis through documented work, organized advocacy, shared smart irrigation infrastructure, and to make women’s labor economically and civically visible.

What comes next

The cascade model from Training 4 is already underway: Three participants have begun teaching neighbors what they learned during our trainings.

The cooperative is going to apply for a joint grant to install a shared smart well system.



The project’s more long-lasting change is harder to measure. When a woman learns to calculate the value of her time, holds up a photograph and says, “This is evidence, and they must answer,” a permanent shift takes place for her individually and the community.



The water in Qyzylsay still disappears every afternoon. But the women who carry it have found their voice.

Nazgul Aidabossynova is a trainer and project coordinator, Digital Voice of Qyzylsay Women in South Kazakhstan, 2026.

This has broad social significance by addressing gender inequality, resource scarcity, and community empowerment with clear context and tangible outcomes.
articles.personality_title: Women in Kazakhstan use smartphones to fight water shortages and gain power
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the village of Qyzylsay, southern Kazakhstan, water stops flowing from taps every afternoon. Women there spend many hours each day fetching and managing water, caring for gardens and livestock, and doing unpaid work that often goes unnoticed.

**What happened** – In 2026, a local trainer named Nazgul led four training sessions called “Digital Voice of Qyzylsay Women.” She taught women how to use their smartphones for more than messaging. They learned to take photos with dates and locations to document water problems and understand their legal rights to water. The women also calculated how much their unpaid work was really worth and explored how smart irrigation could save time and money. This led them to form a cooperative to work together on water issues.

**Impact** – These trainings helped women see their daily work as valuable and gave them tools to hold authorities accountable. By collecting clear evidence of water shortages, they can demand solutions instead of being ignored. The cooperative also plans to install shared smart irrigation systems, which could save them up to 60 hours a month. This is a big change in a community where women’s work was invisible and unpaid.

**What's next step** – Some women are already teaching others what they learned. The cooperative will apply for grants to improve water infrastructure. Over time, this project could inspire other villages to use digital tools for community problems and help women gain economic and civic power.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Women in Qyzylsay are using smartphones and teamwork to turn water shortages into a chance for fair treatment and stronger communities.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des femmes au Kazakhstan utilisent les smartphones pour lutter contre la pénurie d'eau et gagner en pouvoir
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans le village de Qyzylsay, au sud du Kazakhstan, l'eau cesse de couler des robinets chaque après-midi. Les femmes y consacrent de nombreuses heures chaque jour à aller chercher de l'eau, s'occuper des jardins et du bétail, et réaliser un travail non rémunéré souvent invisible.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – En 2026, une formatrice locale nommée Nazgul a animé quatre sessions de formation appelées « Voix numérique des femmes de Qyzylsay ». Elle a appris aux femmes à utiliser leurs smartphones pour plus que la messagerie. Elles ont appris à prendre des photos avec date et localisation pour documenter les problèmes d'eau et comprendre leurs droits légaux à l'eau. Les femmes ont aussi calculé la valeur réelle de leur travail non payé et exploré comment une irrigation intelligente pourrait leur faire gagner du temps et de l'argent. Cela les a amenées à créer une coopérative pour travailler ensemble sur les questions d'eau.

**Impact** – Ces formations ont aidé les femmes à reconnaître la valeur de leur travail quotidien et à disposer d’outils pour demander des comptes aux autorités. En collectant des preuves claires des pénuries d'eau, elles peuvent exiger des solutions au lieu d’être ignorées. La coopérative prévoit aussi d’installer des systèmes d’irrigation intelligents partagés, ce qui pourrait leur faire économiser jusqu’à 60 heures par mois. C’est un grand changement dans une communauté où le travail des femmes était invisible et non rémunéré.

**Prochaines étapes** – Certaines femmes enseignent déjà à leurs voisines ce qu’elles ont appris. La coopérative va demander des subventions pour améliorer les infrastructures d’eau. Avec le temps, ce projet pourrait inspirer d’autres villages à utiliser les outils numériques pour résoudre les problèmes communautaires et aider les femmes à gagner en pouvoir économique et civique.

**En une phrase** – Les femmes de Qyzylsay utilisent les smartphones et le travail collectif pour transformer la pénurie d’eau en une opportunité d’équité et de renforcement des communautés.
articles.personality_title_es: Mujeres en Kazajistán usan teléfonos inteligentes para combatir la escasez de agua y ganar poder
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el pueblo de Qyzylsay, en el sur de Kazajistán, el agua deja de salir de los grifos cada tarde. Las mujeres pasan muchas horas al día recogiendo agua, cuidando jardines y ganado, y realizando trabajo no remunerado que a menudo pasa desapercibido.

**Qué pasó** – En 2026, una formadora local llamada Nazgul dirigió cuatro sesiones de capacitación llamadas “Voz Digital de las Mujeres de Qyzylsay”. Enseñó a las mujeres a usar sus teléfonos inteligentes para más que mensajes. Aprendieron a tomar fotos con fecha y ubicación para documentar problemas de agua y entender sus derechos legales sobre el agua. También calcularon cuánto vale realmente su trabajo no pagado y exploraron cómo la irrigación inteligente podría ahorrarles tiempo y dinero. Esto las llevó a formar una cooperativa para trabajar juntas en los problemas del agua.

**Impacto** – Estas capacitaciones ayudaron a las mujeres a ver su trabajo diario como valioso y les dieron herramientas para exigir responsabilidades a las autoridades. Al recolectar pruebas claras de la escasez de agua, pueden pedir soluciones en lugar de ser ignoradas. La cooperativa también planea instalar sistemas de irrigación inteligentes compartidos, que podrían ahorrarles hasta 60 horas al mes. Esto representa un gran cambio en una comunidad donde el trabajo de las mujeres era invisible y no remunerado.

**Próximo paso** – Algunas mujeres ya están enseñando a otras lo que aprendieron. La cooperativa solicitará subvenciones para mejorar la infraestructura del agua. Con el tiempo, este proyecto podría inspirar a otros pueblos a usar herramientas digitales para resolver problemas comunitarios y ayudar a las mujeres a ganar poder económico y cívico.

**Una frase clave** – Las mujeres de Qyzylsay están usando teléfonos inteligentes y trabajo en equipo para convertir la escasez de agua en una oportunidad para un trato justo y comunidades más fuertes.

articles.title: The firms turning recruitment into X Factor-style competitions
articles.summary: Applicants have to pitch their ideas on stage in front of a panel of judges and an audience. But is this exciting or unfair?
articles.content:
Yumi Liberman was up on stage in front of a panel of judges and an audience of 300 people, and she had to perform.

But rather than singing, dancing or playing a musical instrument, she and two friends were in an auditorium in London in 2024 to pitch their business idea, hoping to secure a full-time job with cosmetics giant L'Oreal.

"It reminded me of when I used to do competitive sports growing up and the pressure would get heavy," says Liberman, now 24. "But somehow you just get into flow mode."

She and her friends had got through to the UK final of Brandstorm, an international competition run by the French company, where young adults outline their product and business ideas.

Their proposal for a haircare app saw them crowned UK winners and they went on to that year's global final in Paris where they came third.

While only members of the team that finished first automatically got full-time jobs, Liberman had so impressed senior figures at the company that she managed to secure a place on its marketing management traineeship, with a full-time position at the end.
articles.reasoning: The article describes an innovative recruitment approach that provides young adults with a platform to showcase their talents and ideas publicly, potentially increasing fairness and opportunity in hiring. It highlights a tangible positive outcome where a participant secured a full-time job through this creative competition, demonstrating meaningful impact on career opportunities for youth.
articles.personality_title: Young people pitch business ideas on stage to win jobs at L'Oréal
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – L'Oréal, a large cosmetics company, runs a competition called Brandstorm. Young people create and share new business ideas to try to win prizes and job opportunities.

**What happened** – In 2024, Yumi Liberman and her two friends took part in the UK final of Brandstorm in London. They presented their idea for a haircare app on stage in front of judges and 300 people. Their team won the UK round and later placed third in the global final in Paris.

**Impact** – This competition gives young people a chance to show their creativity and skills in a public way, different from usual job interviews. Yumi’s performance impressed the company so much that she earned a trainee marketing job at L'Oréal, with a chance for a full-time position later. This shows how creative recruitment can open doors for young talent.

**What's next step** – Yumi will work as a marketing management trainee at L'Oréal, gaining experience that could lead to a permanent role. The company may continue using this competition to find new employees and encourage innovation.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A creative competition helped young people like Yumi turn their business ideas into real job opportunities at a major company.
articles.personality_title_fr: De jeunes talents présentent leurs idées d’entreprise sur scène pour décrocher un emploi chez L'Oréal
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L'Oréal, une grande entreprise de cosmétiques, organise un concours appelé Brandstorm. Des jeunes créent et présentent de nouvelles idées d’entreprise pour gagner des prix et des opportunités d’emploi.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2024, Yumi Liberman et ses deux amies ont participé à la finale britannique de Brandstorm à Londres. Elles ont présenté leur idée d’application pour les soins capillaires devant des juges et 300 personnes. Leur équipe a gagné la finale au Royaume-Uni et a terminé troisième à la finale mondiale à Paris.

**Impact** – Ce concours permet aux jeunes de montrer leur créativité et leurs compétences en public, différemment des entretiens traditionnels. La performance de Yumi a tellement impressionné l’entreprise qu’elle a obtenu un poste de stagiaire en marketing chez L'Oréal, avec la possibilité d’un emploi permanent plus tard. Cela montre comment un recrutement original peut ouvrir des portes.

**Prochaine étape** – Yumi va travailler comme stagiaire en gestion marketing chez L'Oréal pour gagner de l’expérience qui pourrait mener à un poste fixe. L’entreprise pourrait continuer à utiliser ce concours pour recruter et encourager l’innovation.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un concours créatif a aidé des jeunes comme Yumi à transformer leurs idées d’entreprise en véritables opportunités d’emploi dans une grande entreprise.
articles.personality_title_es: Jóvenes presentan ideas de negocio en el escenario para conseguir empleo en L’Oréal
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – L'Oréal, una gran empresa de cosméticos, organiza una competencia llamada Brandstorm. Jóvenes crean y presentan nuevas ideas de negocio para ganar premios y oportunidades de trabajo.

**Qué pasó** – En 2024, Yumi Liberman y sus dos amigas participaron en la final del Reino Unido de Brandstorm en Londres. Presentaron su idea de una aplicación para el cuidado del cabello frente a jueces y 300 personas. Su equipo ganó la ronda del Reino Unido y quedó tercero en la final global en París.

**Impacto** – Esta competencia ofrece a los jóvenes la oportunidad de mostrar su creatividad y habilidades en público, de forma diferente a las entrevistas comunes. La actuación de Yumi impresionó tanto a la empresa que consiguió un puesto de aprendiz en marketing en L'Oréal, con opción a un empleo fijo más adelante. Esto demuestra cómo un reclutamiento creativo puede abrir puertas.

**Próximo paso** – Yumi trabajará como aprendiz en gestión de marketing en L'Oréal para ganar experiencia que podría llevarla a un puesto permanente. La empresa podría seguir usando esta competencia para buscar nuevos empleados y fomentar la innovación.

**Una frase clave** – Una competencia creativa ayudó a jóvenes como Yumi a convertir sus ideas de negocio en oportunidades reales de empleo en una gran empresa.
